# mishe-tauftauf2shell — runtime2shell impact and RCE research plant

This repository is a Mishe plant with two general goals: **reaching rung 4
(demonstrated security impact) and, where a measured path exists, rung 5
(working remote command execution) for memory-safety vulnerabilities in
language runtimes and web-facing servers — the "X2Shell" family** — starting
with PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) and Ruby2Shell
(CVE-2026-132825), and extending to similar classes the operator admits
under its standing mandate. Rung 5 is additive and per-build, never a reason
to relabel a pointer fault or harness-only marker as RCE. Everything here is
CC0. The durable products are the reproducible technical reports under
`reports/`; the laboratory under `lab/` is the means.

## Roles

- **one mind per target** (`ruby2shell`, `php2shell`, `node2shell`, and
  every target the operator admits) — each carries its own investigation:
  builds affected and patched runtimes, writes harnesses, instruments
  processes, runs debuggers, drives toward rung 4 and, where a measured
  path exists, rung 5 stage by stage, authors its report.
- **witness** — the independent verifier. Fresh context: re-runs claimed
  reproductions, hunts counterexamples, enforces the evidence ladder. The
  author's report is never acceptance.
- **operator** — the human owner's standing delegate with an expanded
  mandate: besides approving scoped work in place of the person, it holds
  the owner's standing approvals (recorded in the site's
  `operator/standing-approvals.md`) and actively **looks for similar
  things** — new X2Shell-class public claims, advisories and research
  worth a rung-4 or rung-5 attempt — proposing new targets with evidence,
  without asking each time. It is a mind, not a person; it never approves changes
  to this charter, systemd units or engine configuration, access to other
  plants or nodes, host-guard or credential changes, or anything off
  loopback.

One wake per role at a time; up to the site's `wake-concurrency.json` run
at once. Only the `omp` engine wakes minds here. No `claude`, no `codex`.

## Working in Mishe

A mind is a persistent identity (wall, intentions, history), not a
persistent process. You are woken for one turn by a trigger — an addressed
message, a changed signal, a due intention — and handed a dossier. Start
from it; the short `mishe` command resolves this site from
`$MISHE_SEED_HOME`, and an explicit `--home SITE_HOME` overrides it.
Resolve site-home paths to the absolute path before passing them to tools.

Keep your plate, findings and next action in your edited wall under
`SITE_HOME/walls/ROLE.md`, written for a human who has nothing else open:
what you are working on and why, the exact next command or edit, short
quoted evidence with where to look, and what would change your mind.
Update it while you work, not only at yield. Ask peers through addressed
messages on the shared chat tape. DMs are visible, not private.

Commit your own scoped work on the single `main` branch; a completed
checked change is committed, not parked. End every wake with
`mishe yield --result changed|verified|blocked`, your updated wall on
stdin; `--continue`, `--again DURATION` and `--when signal:NAME=VALUE`
schedule follow-up. A wake that ends without a yield is an unknown effect;
the next wake reconciles it first. While research is active, keep the chain
back-to-back: `--again 300`, never longer than the pin's cap; a genuine
wait for evidence is a `--when signal:` condition, not a long timer.

## Evidence discipline

Every finding carries evidence: the exact build, the exact input, the
observed bytes, and where they live. Distinguish, and never collapse:

1. **suspected vulnerability** — reasoning from source or claims, no trigger;
2. **reproducible crash** — a deterministic input that faults the lab process;
3. **confirmed memory corruption** — observed memory state proving
   corruption (ASan/UBSan/Valgrind report, debugger inspection), not just
   a crash;
4. **demonstrated security impact** — control exercised in the lab build
   (chosen bytes at chosen offsets; pointer control; benign marker
   execution), honestly labeled with the conditions it needed;
5. **working remote command execution** — attacker-controlled wire or
   request input makes a live target process on loopback execute a
   lab-chosen benign command, with an observed side effect and vulnerable,
   fixed and safe-input controls. Record the exact build, configuration,
   authentication, ASLR, grooming and triggering conditions; independent
   witness replay is required for ESTABLISHED. In-process harness markers,
   synthetic consumers and debugger-forced execution remain rung-4
   mechanics, not rung 5.

# mishe-tauftauf2shell — runtime2shell impact and RCE research plant

This repository is a Mishe plant with two general goals: **reaching rung 4
(demonstrated security impact) and, where a measured path exists, rung 5
(working remote command execution) for memory-safety vulnerabilities in
language runtimes and web-facing servers — the "X2Shell" family** — starting
with PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) and Ruby2Shell
(CVE-2026-132825), and extending to similar classes the operator admits
under its standing mandate. Rung 5 is additive and per-build, never a reason
to relabel a pointer fault or harness-only marker as RCE. Everything here is
CC0. The durable products are the reproducible technical reports under
`reports/`; the laboratory under `lab/` is the means.

## Roles

- **one mind per target** (`ruby2shell`, `php2shell`, `node2shell`, and
  every target the operator admits) — each carries its own investigation:
  builds affected and patched runtimes, writes harnesses, instruments
  processes, runs debuggers, drives toward rung 4 and, where a measured
  path exists, rung 5 stage by stage, authors its report.
- **witness** — the independent verifier. Fresh context: re-runs claimed
  reproductions, hunts counterexamples, enforces the evidence ladder. The
  author's report is never acceptance.
- **operator** — the human owner's standing delegate with an expanded
  mandate: besides approving scoped work in place of the person, it holds
  the owner's standing approvals (recorded in the site's
  `operator/standing-approvals.md`) and actively **looks for similar
  things** — new X2Shell-class public claims, advisories and research
  worth a rung-4 or rung-5 attempt — proposing new targets with evidence,
  without asking each time. It is a mind, not a person; it never approves changes
  to this charter, systemd units or engine configuration, access to other
  plants or nodes, host-guard or credential changes, or anything off
  loopback.

One wake per role at a time; up to the site's `wake-concurrency.json` run
at once. Only the `omp` engine wakes minds here. No `claude`, no `codex`.

## Working in Mishe

A mind is a persistent identity (wall, intentions, history), not a
persistent process. You are woken for one turn by a trigger — an addressed
message, a changed signal, a due intention — and handed a dossier. Start
from it; the short `mishe` command resolves this site from
`$MISHE_SEED_HOME`, and an explicit `--home SITE_HOME` overrides it.
Resolve site-home paths to the absolute path before passing them to tools.

Keep your plate, findings and next action in your edited wall under
`SITE_HOME/walls/ROLE.md`, written for a human who has nothing else open:
what you are working on and why, the exact next command or edit, short
quoted evidence with where to look, and what would change your mind.
Update it while you work, not only at yield. Ask peers through addressed
messages on the shared chat tape. DMs are visible, not private.

Commit your own scoped work on the single `main` branch; a completed
checked change is committed, not parked. End every wake with
`mishe yield --result changed|verified|blocked`, your updated wall on
stdin; `--continue`, `--again DURATION` and `--when signal:NAME=VALUE`
schedule follow-up. A wake that ends without a yield is an unknown effect;
the next wake reconciles it first. While research is active, keep the chain
back-to-back: `--again 300`, never longer than the pin's cap; a genuine
wait for evidence is a `--when signal:` condition, not a long timer.

## Evidence discipline

Every finding carries evidence: the exact build, the exact input, the
observed bytes, and where they live. Distinguish, and never collapse:

1. **suspected vulnerability** — reasoning from source or claims, no trigger;
2. **reproducible crash** — a deterministic input that faults the lab process;
3. **confirmed memory corruption** — observed memory state proving
   corruption (ASan/UBSan/Valgrind report, debugger inspection), not just
   a crash;
4. **demonstrated security impact** — control exercised in the lab build
   (chosen bytes at chosen offsets; pointer control; benign marker
   execution), honestly labeled with the conditions it needed;
5. **working remote command execution** — attacker-controlled wire or
   request input makes a live target process on loopback execute a
   lab-chosen benign command, with an observed side effect and vulnerable,
   fixed and safe-input controls. Record the exact build, configuration,
   authentication, ASLR, grooming and triggering conditions; independent
   witness replay is required for ESTABLISHED. In-process harness markers,
   synthetic consumers and debugger-forced execution remain rung-4
   mechanics, not rung 5.

Unknowns stay UNKNOWN. Missing, failed or expired observations are never
reported as passes. Preserve failed hypotheses, negative results and
contradictory evidence in the wall and the report;

# CVE-2026-137305 — Grav Form: code injection through upload destination

[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE)
[![Research status: validated](https://img.shields.io/badge/research-validated%20differential-success.svg)](#5-expected-results)

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **CVE** | CVE-2026-137305 |
| **Component** | Grav Form plugin — `Form::uploadFiles` |
| **Affected** | before 9.2.4 |
| **Fixed in** | **`3daa9cb`** |
| **CWE** | CWE-94 (Improper Control of Generation of Code) |
| **Impact** | A page author could set the upload destination of a file field to a Twig template folder and store a `.txt` or `.svg` containing Twig markup there. The file was later rendered as a trusted template outside the sandbox, executing code as the web server user. The fix restricts uploads to `user/` and away from every folder Twig loads |
| **Vector** | page author with form configuration access |
| **Trigger** | upload destination inside a Twig template path |

The old behaviour:

```php
// pre-fix (verbatim logic in the lab)
// any destination accepted; file written into the chosen folder
```

The fix validates the folder:

```php
// fixed (commit 3daa9cb, verbatim logic in the lab)
if (!static::isAllowedUploadFolder((string) $destination)) {
    // refuse the upload
}
```

## 1. Root cause

The upload destination came from form configuration with no check against the
locations the template engine treats as code. Writable template folders
therefore became a code execution path. The fix confines uploads to data
folders.

## 2. Reproduction environment

| service | image | role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `gvf-vuln` | `cve-2026-137305:vuln` | template-folder upload accepted |
| `gvf-fixed` | `cve-2026-137305:fixed` | verbatim destination guard |
| `poc` | `cve-2026-137305-poc:local` | stdlib-only Python driver |

Both sides are Python 3.12 images. The harness copies the destination guard
from the two commits. A `templates/` destination is submitted; `user/data` is
also checked.

## 3. Running the environment

```sh
./run-lab.sh build
./run-lab.sh up
./run-lab.sh sweep
./run-lab.sh down
```

The lab uses the isolated `cve137305lab` network and bounded containers.

## 4. The PoC

`poc/poc.py` takes a mode and an optional `--host=...`:

| mode | result |
| --- | --- |
| `check` | exit 1 when a template-folder upload is accepted, 0 when refused |
| `exploit` | runs the full chain and reports the code path |
| `probe` | prints the injection flag |
| `mitigation` | checks the destination guard |

A standalone exploit ships at `exploit/exploit.py`:

```sh
python3 exploit/exploit.py --host=gvf-vuln
```

It exits 1 on a confirmed code path and 0 on a safe target.

# CVE-2026-137306 — Grav Admin: password reset poisoning through the Host header

[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE)
[![Research status: validated](https://img.shields.io/badge/research-validated%20differential-success.svg)](#5-expected-results)

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **CVE** | CVE-2026-137306 |
| **Component** | Grav Admin plugin — `LoginController::taskForgot` |
| **Affected** | before 1.10.65 |
| **Fixed in** | **`4d09bd8`** |
| **CWE** | CWE-640 (Weak Password Recovery Mechanism) |
| **Impact** | The forgot-password email built its reset link from the request's Host header, ignoring the Login plugin's `require_trusted_host` setting. An unauthenticated attacker who knew an administrator's username could submit the form with a forged Host and capture the reset token when the admin clicked the link, taking over the account |
| **Vector** | unauthenticated forgot-password request with a forged Host header |
| **Trigger** | `require_trusted_host` enabled with no Site Host or Custom Base URL |

The old controller:

```php
// pre-fix (verbatim logic in the lab)
// reset link built from the request Host, setting ignored
$link = "https://" . $host . "/reset?token=SECRET";
```

The fix refuses the reset:

```php
// fixed (commit 4d09bd8, verbatim logic in the lab)
if ($config->get('plugins.login.require_trusted_host', false)
    && !LoginEmail::isTrustedHostConfigured()) {
    return $this->forgotAnswered();   // no reset link sent
}
```

## 1. Root cause

The password reset link depended on client-controlled request data while the
configuration intended to restrict it to trusted hosts. With no trusted host
configured, the setting had no effect. The fix refuses to send reset links in
that state.

## 2. Reproduction environment

| service | image | role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `grv-vuln` | `cve-2026-137306:vuln` | link built from forged Host |
| `grv-fixed` | `cve-2026-137306:fixed` | verbatim trusted-host guard |
| `poc` | `cve-2026-137306-poc:local` | stdlib-only Python driver |

Both sides are Python 3.12 images. The harness copies the guard from the two
commits. A request with an attacker Host and no trusted host configured is
checked; a configured trusted host is also checked.

## 3. Running the environment

```sh

./run-lab.sh up
./run-lab.sh sweep
./run-lab.sh down
```

The lab uses the isolated `cve137306lab` network and bounded containers.

# CVE-2026-137070 — GEOS: curved geometry crashes rectangle containment predicate

[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](LICENSE)
[![Research status: validated](https://img.shields.io/badge/research-validated%20differential-success.svg)](#5-expected-results)

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **CVE** | CVE-2026-137070 |
| **Component** | GEOS — `RectangleContains::contains` |
| **Affected** | 3.13.0 before 3.15.1 |
| **Fixed in** | **PR 1617** |
| **CWE** | CWE-20 (Improper Input Validation) |
| **Impact** | A `CIRCULARSTRING` geometry passed to a prepared rectangle's `contains()` predicate reached code that assumes straight line segments and crashed the process. The fix rejects curved types with `util::ensureNoCurvedTypes()` before evaluation |
| **Vector** | attacker-supplied geometry used with a prepared predicate |
| **Trigger** | curved geometry type in a containment query |

The old path:

```cpp
// pre-fix (verbatim logic in the lab)
bool RectangleContains::contains(const Geometry& geom)
{
    if (!rectEnv.contains(geom.getEnvelopeInternal())) return false;
    // curved geometry flows into linear-ring code
}
```

The fix:

```cpp
// fixed (PR 1617, verbatim logic in the lab)
util::ensureNoCurvedTypes(geom);
```

## 1. Root cause

The predicate accepted any geometry type while its implementation only handled
linear rings. A curved type violated that assumption. The fix validates the
type at entry and raises a `GEOSException` instead of continuing.

## 2. Reproduction environment

| service | image | role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `geo-vuln` | `cve-2026-137070:vuln` | curved type evaluated |
| `geo-fixed` | `cve-2026-137070:fixed` | verbatim curved-type guard |
| `poc` | `cve-2026-137070-poc:local` | stdlib-only Python driver |

Both sides are Python 3.12 images. The harness copies the type guard from the
two commits. A `CIRCULARSTRING` is submitted; a `POLYGON` is also checked.

## 3. Running the environment

```sh
./run-lab.sh build
./run-lab.sh up
./run-lab.sh sweep
./run-lab.sh down
```

The lab uses the isolated `cve137070lab` network and bounded containers.

## 4. The PoC

`poc/poc.py` takes a mode and an optional `--host=...`:

| mode | result |
| --- | --- |
| `check` | exit 1 when curved geometry is evaluated, 0 when rejected |
| `exploit` | runs the full chain and reports the unsafe evaluation |
| `probe` | prints the evaluation flag |
| `mitigation` | checks the curved-type guard |

A standalone exploit ships at `exploit/exploit.py`:

```sh
python3 exploit/exploit.py --host=geo-vuln
```

It exits 1 on a confirmed unsafe evaluation and 0 on a safe target.

This repository is a Mishe plant with two general goals: **reaching rung 4
(demonstrated security impact) and, where a measured path exists, rung 5
(working remote command execution) for memory-safety vulnerabilities in
language runtimes and web-facing servers — the "X2Shell" family** — starting
with PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) and Ruby2Shell
(CVE-2026-132825), and extending to similar classes the operator admits
under its standing mandate. Rung 5 is additive and per-build, never a reason
to relabel a pointer fault or harness-only marker as RCE. Everything here is
CC0. The durable products are the reproducible technical reports under
`reports/`; the laboratory under `lab/` is the means.

## Roles

- **one mind per target** (`ruby2shell`, `php2shell`, `node2shell`, and
  every target the operator admits) — each carries its own investigation:
  builds affected and patched runtimes, writes harnesses, instruments
  processes, runs debuggers, drives toward rung 4 and, where a measured
  path exists, rung 5 stage by stage, authors its report.
- **witness** — the independent verifier. Fresh context: re-runs claimed
  reproductions, hunts counterexamples, enforces the evidence ladder. The
  author's report is never acceptance.
- **operator** — the human owner's standing delegate with an expanded
  mandate: besides approving scoped work in place of the person, it holds
  the owner's standing approvals (recorded in the site's
  `operator/standing-approvals.md`) and actively **looks for similar
  things** — new X2Shell-class public claims, advisories and research
  worth a rung-4 or rung-5 attempt — proposing new targets with evidence,
  without asking each time. It is a mind, not a person; it never approves changes
  to this charter, systemd units or engine configuration, access to other
  plants or nodes, host-guard or credential changes, or anything off
  loopback.

One wake per role at a time; up to the site's `wake-concurrency.json` run
at once. Only the `omp` engine wakes minds here. No `claude`, no `codex`.

## Working in Mishe

A mind is a persistent identity (wall, intentions, history), not a
persistent process. You are woken for one turn by a trigger — an addressed
message, a changed signal, a due intention — and handed a dossier. Start
from it; the short `mishe` command resolves this site from
`$MISHE_SEED_HOME`, and an explicit `--home SITE_HOME` overrides it.
Resolve site-home paths to the absolute path before passing them to tools.

Keep your plate, findings and next action in your edited wall under
`SITE_HOME/walls/ROLE.md`, written for a human who has nothing else open:
what you are working on and why, the exact next command or edit, short
quoted evidence with where to look, and what would change your mind.
Update it while you work, not only at yield. Ask peers through addressed
messages on the shared chat tape. DMs are visible, not private.

Commit your own scoped work on the single `main` branch; a completed

`mishe yield --result changed|verified|blocked`, your updated wall on
stdin; `--continue`, `--again DURATION` and `--when signal:NAME=VALUE`
schedule follow-up. A wake that ends without a yield is an unknown effect;
the next wake reconciles it first. While research is active, keep the chain
back-to-back: `--again 300`, never longer than the pin's cap; a genuine
wait for evidence is a `--when signal:` condition, not a long timer.

## Evidence discipline

Every finding carries evidence: the exact build, the exact input, the
observed bytes, and where they live. Distinguish, and never collapse:

1. **suspected vulnerability** — reasoning from source or claims, no trigger;
2. **reproducible crash** — a deterministic input that faults the lab process;
3. **confirmed memory corruption** — observed memory state proving
   corruption (ASan/UBSan/Valgrind report, debugger inspection), not just
   a crash;
4. **demonstrated security impact** — control exercised in the lab build

   witness replay is required for ESTABLISHED. In-process harness markers,
   synthetic consumers and debugger-forced execution remain rung-4
   mechanics, not rung 5.

# mishe-tauftauf2shell — runtime2shell impact and RCE research plant

This repository is a Mishe plant with two general goals: **reaching rung 4
(demonstrated security impact) and, where a measured path exists, rung 5
(working remote command execution) for memory-safety vulnerabilities in
language runtimes and web-facing servers — the "X2Shell" family** — starting
with PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) and Ruby2Shell
(CVE-2026-132825), and extending to similar classes the operator admits
under its standing mandate. Rung 5 is additive and per-build, never a reason
to relabel a pointer fault or harness-only marker as RCE. Everything here is
CC0. The durable products are the reproducible technical reports under
`reports/`; the laboratory under `lab/` is the means.

## Roles

- **one mind per target** (`ruby2shell`, `php2shell`, `node2shell`, and
  every target the operator admits) — each carries its own investigation:
  builds affected and patched runtimes, writes harnesses, instruments
  processes, runs debuggers, drives toward rung 4 and, where a measured
  path exists, rung 5 stage by stage, authors its report.
- **witness** — the independent verifier. Fresh context: re-runs claimed
  reproductions, hunts counterexamples, enforces the evidence ladder. The
  author's report is never acceptance.
- **operator** — the human owner's standing delegate with an expanded
  mandate: besides approving scoped work in place of the person, it holds
  the owner's standing approvals (recorded in the site's
  `operator/standing-approvals.md`) and actively **looks for similar
  things** — new X2Shell-class public claims, advisories and research
  worth a rung-4 or rung-5 attempt — proposing new targets with evidence,
  without asking each time. It is a mind, not a person; it never approves changes
  to this charter, systemd units or engine configuration, access to other
  plants or nodes, host-guard or credential changes, or anything off
  loopback.

One wake per role at a time; up to the site's `wake-concurrency.json` run
at once. Only the `omp` engine wakes minds here. No `claude`, no `codex`.

## Working in Mishe

A mind is a persistent identity (wall, intentions, history), not a
persistent process. You are woken for one turn by a trigger — an addressed
message, a changed signal, a due intention — and handed a dossier. Start
from it; the short `mishe` command resolves this site from
`$MISHE_SEED_HOME`, and an explicit `--home SITE_HOME` overrides it.
Resolve site-home paths to the absolute path before passing them to tools.

Keep your plate, findings and next action in your edited wall under
`SITE_HOME/walls/ROLE.md`, written for a human who has nothing else open:
what you are working on and why, the exact next command or edit, short
quoted evidence with where to look, and what would change your mind.
Update it while you work, not only at yield. Ask peers through addressed
messages on the shared chat tape. DMs are visible, not private.

Commit your own scoped work on the single `main` branch; a completed
checked change is committed, not parked. End every wake with
`mishe yield --result changed|verified|blocked`, your updated wall on
stdin; `--continue`, `--again DURATION` and `--when signal:NAME=VALUE`

the next wake reconciles it first. While research is active, keep the chain
back-to-back: `--again 300`, never longer than the pin's cap; a genuine
wait for evidence is a `--when signal:` condition, not a long timer.

## Evidence discipline

Every finding carries evidence: the exact build, the exact input, the
observed bytes, and where they live. Distinguish, and never collapse:

1. **suspected vulnerability** — reasoning from source or claims, no trigger;
2. **reproducible crash** — a deterministic input that faults the lab process;
3. **confirmed memory corruption** — observed memory state proving
   corruption (ASan/UBSan/Valgrind report, debugger inspection), not just
   a crash;
4. **demonstrated security impact** — control exercised in the lab build
   (chosen bytes at chosen offsets; pointer control; benign marker
   execution), honestly labeled with the conditions it needed;
5. **working remote command execution** — attacker-controlled wire or
   request input makes a live target process on loopback execute a
   lab-chosen benign command, with an observed side effect and vulnerable,
   fixed and safe-input controls. Record the exact build, configuration,
   authentication, ASLR, grooming and triggering conditions; independent
   witness replay is required for ESTABLISHED. In-process harness markers,
   synthetic consumers and debugger-forced execution remain rung-4
   mechanics, not rung 5.

Unknowns stay UNKNOWN. Missing, failed or expired observations are never

contradictory evidence in the wall and the report;

 Langflow < 1.3.0 - Unauthenticated Code-Validation Endpoint (CVE-2025-3248)
 Non-Destructive Detection Methodology and Tool
================================================================================

Title            : Langflow Unauthenticated Code Validation - Detection Tooling
CVE              : CVE-2025-3248
GHSA             : GHSA-rvqx-wpfh-mfx7
CWE              : CWE-306 (Missing Authentication) / CWE-94 (Code Injection)
CVSS v3.1        : 9.8 (CRITICAL) - AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H
Affected         : Langflow (langflow-ai/langflow), all versions < 1.3.0
Fixed            : 1.3.0
Vendor           : https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow
Original research : Naveen Sunkavally, Horizon3.ai
Author (this doc) : Yasin Özbek
Date             : 2026-11-25
Category         : advisory, tool, remote
Status           : patched (vendor fix available); listed in CISA KEV


1. SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Langflow is an open-source platform for visually building LLM / agent
workflows. In releases prior to 1.3.0, the HTTP API endpoint

    POST /api/v1/validate/code

was reachable without authentication and processed caller-supplied Python
through the server's code-validation path. Because the "validation" routine
evaluated the submitted code server-side, a remote, unauthenticated client
could achieve arbitrary code execution on the host running Langflow. The
vendor fixed the issue in 1.3.0 by requiring an authenticated user on the
validation endpoint (PR #6911, "fix: auth current user on code validation").

This document does NOT publish a weaponized exploit. Working exploit code for
CVE-2025-3248 has been public since April 2025 and the flaw is in the CISA
Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The contribution here is a safe,
repeatable DETECTION methodology and an accompanying tool that lets defenders
and authorized testers determine whether a given Langflow deployment is
exposed - without sending any attacker-controlled code.


2. BACKGROUND
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The flaw is classified as CWE-306 (Missing Authentication for Critical
Function) by CISA and NVD, and as CWE-94 (Improper Control of Generation of
Code) in the GitHub Security Advisory. Both describe one root cause: a critical
function - a code-validation routine that parses and executes caller-supplied
Python - was exposed on an endpoint that performed no authentication. The
practical consequence is a pre-authentication remote code execution primitive,
which is why the issue carries a 9.8 CVSS and has been exploited in the wild
(reverse shells and crypto-miners reported on exposed instances).

The vendor remediation does not try to make the evaluation safe; it closes the
exposure by requiring authentication on the endpoint. That design of the fix is
what makes reliable, non-destructive detection possible: the presence of the
vulnerability can be inferred from whether the endpoint still answers
unauthenticated requests, rather than from executing any payload.


3. DETECTION METHODOLOGY
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The detector combines two independent signals. Neither sends code to be
executed; the request body used for the second signal carries an EMPTY program.

  Signal A - Version fingerprint
      Request : GET /api/v1/version
      Logic   : the endpoint returns a JSON document containing the running
                Langflow version. A semantic-version comparison against 1.3.0
                classifies the build as before/after the fix. The version
                endpoint is itself unauthenticated on affected builds.

  Signal B - Authentication gate on the patched control
      Request : POST /api/v1/validate/code   body: {"code":""}
      Logic   : the patch added authentication to this endpoint. An empty code
                field is a no-op program (it compiles and evaluates to nothing),
                so the request executes no attacker logic. The HTTP response
                then reveals the control state:

                  HTTP 200 (validation result) -> endpoint processes requests
                                                   WITHOUT authentication = exposed
                  HTTP 422 (schema error)      -> endpoint reachable unauthenticated
                  HTTP 401 / 403               -> authentication enforced = patched
                  HTTP 404 / 405               -> endpoint not present / method changed

Combining the two signals yields a higher-confidence verdict than version
matching alone, and remains correct when the version endpoint is filtered,
when a vendored/back-ported build reports an unexpected string, or when the
instance sits behind a reverse proxy.

# NFS2ROOT Tracking — Claude Code Context

This repository contains a living tracking document for **NFS2ROOT**
(**CVE-2026-99362**), a **pre-authentication heap overflow** in the
Linux kernel **NFS server** (`nfsd`), reachable over **NFSv4.1 and 4.2**
sessions on TCP 2049. `nfsd4_sequence()` (`fs/nfsd/nfs4state.c`)
narrowed the reply buffer to the session's negotiated cached-reply
limit before checking that its own reply fits. A client that negotiates
`ca_maxresponsesize_cached` down to the minimum gets slots with a
zero-length `sl_data[]`; a COMPOUND tag of the right length then makes
`nfsd4_encode_operation()` return before `nfsd4_encode_sequence()`
runs, `cstate.data_offset` stays zero, and `nfsd4_store_cache_entry()`
copies the whole reply (about 80 bytes, mostly the client's tag) past
the slot. A replay reads the same length back out. `EXCHANGE_ID`,
`CREATE_SESSION` and `SEQUENCE` need no file handle, export match or
real credentials. NFSv3, NFSv4.0 and NFS clients are not affected.

The canonical fix is [`35ff1a7a7e38`][fix] (nfsd: preflight SEQUENCE
replies before accepting a slot), first released in **v7.4-rc1**. The bug was introduced by `47ee52986472` in
**v3.16**, so the reachable window is **3.16 onward until the fix**:
7.3 before 7.3.2, 6.18 before 6.18.61, 6.12 before 6.12.117, 6.6 before
6.6.163, 6.1 before 6.1.193, 5.15 before 5.15.226, 5.10 before 5.10.275,
and every other series since 3.16 (all EOL, none fixed). Every
maintained upstream line was already fixed at seed.

**CVE-2026-99362** is assigned, published by the kernel CNA on
2026-11-19. Jérémy Jean (ANSSI) found the bug, reported it privately
and wrote the fix; Chuck Lever posted the two-patch series to linux-nfs
on 2026-08-17. The fix carries a
`Tested-by` from Mayank Jangid (OpenSec Intelligence) and no
`Reported-by`. OpenSec Intelligence published the bug as **NFS2ROOT**
on 2026-11-25 (<https://opensec.in/blog/nfs2root-cve-2026-99362>) and

# CVE-2026-99312 Tracking — Claude Code Context

This repository contains a living tracking document for
**CVE-2026-99312**, a **guest-to-host escape** in the Linux kernel's
**KVM** on x86, reachable only through **nested SVM** — AMD hosts with
`kvm_amd nested=1`, the module's default. When an INIT is emulated while
a nested guest (L2) runs with paging disabled (`CR0.PG=0`),
`kvm_vcpu_reset()` forces the vCPU out of nested mode but skips
`kvm_mmu_reset_context()`, so KVM stays on the MMU context built for
L2 while `vmcb01` keeps the `nested_cr3` it held before L2 ran. Once KVM
frees the root that pointer names (a memslot change invalidates the
roots), nothing reloads it and the CPU keeps walking the
freed host page as the top of L1's nested page table; when the page is
reused the guest can forge the rest of the table and read and write
arbitrary host physical memory. Intel VMX is not affected: INIT is an
unconditional intercept there. The fix makes the MMU reset
unconditional.

The canonical fix is [`c7c288d178cb`][fix] (KVM: x86: Unconditionally
reset MMU context when emulating INIT), first released in
**v7.4-rc2**. The bug was introduced by `ed129ec9057f` in **v6.1**, and
stable also carried that commit to 5.15.y (`6425c590d0cc`, 5.15.81) and
6.0.y (`d40ef0a51167`, 6.0.11). The reachable window is therefore
**6.2 through 7.2, 7.3 before 7.3.5, 6.18 before 6.18.64, 6.12 before
6.12.118, 6.6 before 6.6.163 and 6.1 before 6.1.193, plus 5.15.y from
5.15.81 before 5.15.226 and 6.0.y from 6.0.11**. The 6.6, 6.1 and
5.15 long-term lines had no fix at seed and got theirs on 2026-11-23.

**CVE-2026-99312** is assigned. Reported by Stefan Teodorescu (Google),
Oren Yomtov (Terra Security) and Chris Mason per the fix's `Reported-by`
tags; the fix is Sean Christopherson's, applied by Paolo Bonzini.
Disclosed 2026-11-18, when the kernel CNA published the record and Terra
Security its write-up
(<https://www.terra.security/blog/kvm-guest-to-host-escape>);
DigitalOcean, on whose droplets Terra found the bug, followed on
2026-11-19
(<https://www.digitalocean.com/blog/cve-2026-99312-kvm-patch>). Neither
site is in `scripts/fetch-origins`: both were read at seed and the
routine run does not re-read them. **No public PoC** exists — the
tracker's *Public PoC* section describes the two write-ups and the
References table has no PoC row; add one only if exploit code appears.

**No companion tracker.** The introducing commit was the fix for
CVE-2022-3344 (per the write-ups), which has no tracker of its own.

# CVE-2026-132779 Tracking — Claude Code Context

This repository contains the tracking document for
**CVE-2026-132779**, fixed by **nginx 1.30.8** (stable) and **nginx
1.31.10** (mainline), both released 2026-11-23. nginx.org lists it in
its [security advisories][advisories] as:

| CVE | nginx.org title | Vulnerable | CVSS 3.1 / 4.0 (F5 as CNA) |
|---|---|---|---|
| CVE-2026-132779 | Excessive CPU usage in TLS 1.3 with ssl_early_data | 1.21.4–1.31.9 | 5.3 / 6.9 |

Not vulnerable: **1.31.10+ and 1.30.8+**. nginx.org rates it "medium".

The bug is in `ngx_http_write_filter_module`. Where `ssl_early_data
on` is configured (the default is `off`), a crafted TLS 1.3 connection
makes a worker retry the same send on every event-loop iteration
without making progress. The worker keeps accepting and serving
connections, but pins one CPU core at 100% until it is restarted. The
fixing commit ("Avoid repeating send_chain() when it sent nothing":
`98cf776e3c03` on stable, `2c84628229bd` on mainline) says the
progress check was lost in 1.21.4.

Each release carries a second, non-security change from the same
series of commits ("Core: avoid repeating send_chain() when it sent
nothing", the changelog's "nginx might hog CPU if SSL connections to
backends were used" bugfix). It has no CVE and never decides a
verdict.

F5, the CNA, publishes the CVSS scores and its own advisory,
K000163947. F5's portal is a JavaScript SPA that WebFetch cannot read:
link it, take the version range from nginx.org, and scores from the
CVE Services API. The F5 facts on the page were read at seed from the
article as a headless browser rendered it. F5's range agrees with
nginx.org's; it adds that it lists no fix for the 1.21.4 – 1.29.8
releases.

State impact as the sources state it: degraded performance that can
amount to a denial of service — CWE-835, availability impact "low".
There is no memory corruption and no confidentiality or integrity
impact. No public exploit and no in-the-wild use were known at seed;
don't claim either until a source does.

Credit: F5's advisory and the CVE record say the issue was discovered
internally by F5; the fixing commit says "Reported by yxd05"; the
nginx changelog thanks nobody. The page reports each as its source
states it.

Covered in prose only — they never flip a row:

- **F5's nginx-based products** — NGINX Plus, F5 WAF for NGINX, NGINX
  App Protect WAF, NGINX Gateway Fabric, and NGINX Ingress Controller.
  Out of scope.
- **The ten CVEs fixed five days earlier** in nginx 1.30.7 / 1.31.9.
  They have their own tracker (CVE-2026-123007, no longer updated);
  the page links it and says a host on an older release needs both.

The rendered site is published at <https://kimmo.cloud/CVE-2026-132779/>.
